concepts.title: Learning as a Meta-Algorithm
concepts.one_liner: Learning is a meta-algorithm that extracts lessons from past experience to search for and output an algorithm that solves future problems.
concepts.content:
The goal of learning is to extract lessons from past experience in order to solve future problems. Typically, this involves searching for an algorithm that solves past instances of the problem. This algorithm can then be applied to future instances of the problem. In this context, past and future do not necessarily refer to calendar dates; instead, they refer to what the learner has previously seen and what the learner will see next. Because learning is itself an algorithm, it can be understood as a meta-algorithm: an algorithm that outputs algorithms.

(see figure: Learning is an algorithm that outputs algorithms.)
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing learning as a meta-algorithm helps formalize the process of automated problem-solving. It frames the learner's task as a search for a functional mapping that generalizes from known data to unknown future instances.
concepts.recap_md: - Learning extracts lessons from past experience to solve future problems.

concepts.title: Training Phase
concepts.one_liner: The training phase is the stage of learning where an algorithm is sought that performs well on past instances of a problem.
concepts.content: Learning usually consists of two phases. In the training phase, we search for an algorithm that performs well on past instances of the problem, which are referred to as training data.
concepts.motivation_md: To solve new problems, a system must first find a pattern or rule that works on known data. The training phase is the dedicated process of searching for this rule.
concepts.recap_md: - The training phase involves searching for an algorithm using past problem instances.

concepts.title: Testing Phase
concepts.one_liner: The testing phase is the stage where a learned algorithm is deployed to solve new instances of a problem.
concepts.content: Learning usually consists of two phases. Following the training phase, the testing phase is where we deploy our learned algorithm to solve new instances of the problem.
concepts.motivation_md: The ultimate goal of learning is generalization. The testing phase evaluates how well the algorithm performs on data it has never seen before, simulating real-world deployment.
concepts.recap_md: - The testing phase deploys a learned algorithm on new problem instances.

concepts.title: Supervised Learning
concepts.one_liner: Supervised learning is the process of inferring a functional mapping by observing example input-output pairs.
concepts.content:
Learning from examples is also called supervised learning. In this context, an algorithm is a computable mapping from inputs to outputs, and an example is formally defined as an {`input`, `output`} pair. For instance, a learner might be given pairs such as:

$$\begin{aligned} &\{\texttt{input:} [2,3], \texttt{output:} 36\}\nonumber \\ &\{\texttt{input:} [7,1], \texttt{output:} 49\}\nonumber \\ &\{\texttt{input:} [5,2], \texttt{output:} 100\}\nonumber \\ &\{\texttt{input:} [2,2], \texttt{output:}16\}\nonumber \end{aligned}$$

This kind of learning, where you observe example input-output behavior and infer a functional mapping that explains this behavior, is called supervised learning.
concepts.motivation_md: Supervised learning is used when we have a set of labeled data and want to automate the process of predicting the output for new, unlabeled inputs by learning the underlying rule.
concepts.recap_md: - Supervised learning involves learning a mapping from inputs to outputs using labeled examples.

slots.motivation: Supervised learning is used when we have a set of labeled data and want to automate the process of predicting the output for new, unlabeled inputs by learning the underlying rule.
slots.key_passage: - Supervised learning involves learning a mapping from inputs to outputs using labeled examples.

concepts.title: Learnability and Noncomputable Functions
concepts.one_liner: Noncomputable functions cannot be perfectly learned from examples because no algorithm can solve them in finite time.
concepts.content: Some things are not learnable from examples, such as noncomputable functions. An example of a noncomputable function is a function that takes as input a program and outputs a 1 if the program will eventually finish running, and a 0 if it will run forever. It is noncomputable because there is no algorithm that can solve this task in finite time. However, it might be possible to learn a good approximation to it.
concepts.motivation_md: It is important to understand the theoretical limits of machine learning. Recognizing that some functions are noncomputable helps define the boundaries of what can be perfectly solved versus what can only be approximated.
concepts.recap_md: - Noncomputable functions lack an algorithm that can solve them in finite time.

concepts.title: Fitting a Model
concepts.one_liner: Fitting a model is an alternative name for learning from data.
concepts.content: Another name for this kind of learning is fitting a model to data.
concepts.motivation_md: This terminology connects machine learning to statistical traditions, where the goal is to find parameters for a mathematical structure (the model) that best represent the observed data.
concepts.recap_md: - Fitting a model is synonymous with learning from data.

concepts.title: Unsupervised Learning
concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised learning involves creating a model of input data that optimizes an objective function without being given target outputs.
concepts.content: Even without examples, we can still learn. Instead of matching input-output examples, we can try to come up with an algorithm that optimizes for desirable properties of the input-output mapping. This class of learners includes unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning. In unsupervised learning, we are given examples of input data $\{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$ but we are not told the target outputs $\{y^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$. Instead, the learner has to come up with a model or representation of the input data that has useful properties, as measured by some objective function. The objective could be, for example, to compress the data into a lower dimensional format that still preserves all information about the inputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Unsupervised learning is essential when labeled data is unavailable or expensive. It allows us to discover hidden structures, patterns, or efficient representations within raw data automatically.
concepts.recap_md: - Unsupervised learning uses input data without corresponding target outputs.

concepts.title: Probability Mass Function (pmf)
concepts.one_liner: A probability mass function (pmf) over K classes is a K-dimensional vector with elements in the range [0,1] that sum to 1.
concepts.content: A probability mass function (pmf) $\mathbf{p}$ over $K$ classes is defined as a $K$-dimensional vector with elements in the range $[0,1]$ that sums to 1. In other words, $\mathbf{p}$ is a point on the $(K-1)$-simplex, which we denote as $\mathbf{p} \in \vartriangle^{K-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: To interpret a model's output as a valid probability distribution across multiple categories, the output must satisfy the mathematical constraints of a probability mass function.
concepts.recap_md:
- A pmf is a vector of probabilities for discrete classes.
 - Elements must be in the range $[0,1]$ and sum to exactly 1.
 - Geometrically, a pmf exists as a point on a $(K-1)$-simplex.

concepts.title: (K-1)-Simplex
concepts.one_liner: The (K-1)-simplex is the set of all K-dimensional vectors whose elements sum to 1.

concepts.title: Softmax Function
concepts.one_liner: The softmax function squashes a vector of real numbers into a valid probability mass function.
concepts.content:
To ensure that the output of a learned function $f_{\theta}$ represents a valid probability mass function, i.e., $f_{\theta} \in \vartriangle^{K-1}$, we can compose two steps: (1) first apply a function $z_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^K$, (2) then squash the output into the range $[0,1]$ and normalize it to sum to 1. A popular way to squash is via the softmax function:

$$\begin{aligned}
    &\mathbf{z} = z_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\\
    &\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \texttt{softmax}(\mathbf{z})\\
    &\quad \quad \hat{y}_j = \frac{e^{-z_j}}{\sum_{i=1}^K e^{-z_k}}.
\end{aligned}$$

Using softmax is a modeling choice; any function that squashes into a valid pmf (a nonnegative vector that sums to 1) could be used.
concepts.motivation_md: Neural networks typically output arbitrary real numbers, but classification requires a probability distribution. Softmax provides a differentiable way to map these real values to probabilities.
concepts.recap_md:
- Softmax squashes $K$ real-valued inputs into the range $[0,1]$.
 - The resulting vector is normalized to sum to 1, forming a valid pmf.
 - It is a common modeling choice for multi-class classification outputs.

concepts.title: Logits
concepts.one_liner: Logits are unnormalized log probabilities of each class.
concepts.content: The values in the vector $\mathbf{z}$ are called the logits and can be interpreted as the unnormalized log probabilities of each class.
concepts.motivation_md: Logits represent the raw scores produced by a model before they are constrained into a probability distribution, allowing for easier mathematical manipulation in optimization.
concepts.recap_md:
- Logits are the raw output values before the softmax transformation.
 - They represent unnormalized log probabilities.

concepts.title: Metalearning
concepts.one_liner: Metalearning, or learning to learn, is a special case of learning where the hypothesis space consists of learning algorithms.
concepts.content:
Learning to learn, also called metalearning, is a special case of learning where the hypothesis space is learning algorithms. While standard learners train on past instances to solve future instances, metalearning handles cases where the future problem is itself a learning problem, such as finding a least-squares line fit to data. 

For example, given sets of input-output pairs representing regression tasks:
$$\begin{aligned}
    &\{\texttt{input:} \big(x:[1,2], y:[1,2]\big), &&\texttt{output:} y = x\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} \big(x:[1,2], y:[2,4]\big), &&\texttt{output:} y = 2x\}\nonumber \\
    &\{\texttt{input:} \big(x:[1,2], y:[0.5,1]\big), &&\texttt{output:} y = \frac{x}{2}\}\nonumber
\end{aligned}$$
A learner can fit these examples by learning to perform least-squares regression. Since least-squares regression is itself a learning algorithm, the learner has learned to learn. 

Learning is a meta-algorithm (an algorithm that outputs an algorithm), making metalearning a meta-meta-algorithm. This can be visualized by adding an outer loop to a learner.

(see figure: Learning is a meta-algorithm, an algorithm that outputs algorithms; metalearning is just learning applied to learning, and therefore it is a meta-meta-algorithm.)

This idea can be applied recursively. Humans perform multiple levels of this: we have evolved to be taught how to learn quickly.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard learning is limited to specific tasks; metalearning aims to create systems that can adapt to new tasks more efficiently by leveraging experience from a variety of previous learning problems.
concepts.recap_md:
- Metalearning treats learning algorithms themselves as the hypothesis space.
 - It is a "meta-meta-algorithm" that outputs a learning algorithm.
 - It can be applied recursively, as seen in human evolution and education.

concepts.title: Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM)

position.section_title: Empirical Risk Minimization: A Formalization of Learning from Examples

concepts.one_liner: Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) is a framework for supervised learning that seeks to minimize the average loss incurred over a set of training examples.
concepts.motivation_md: ERM provides a formal mathematical framework to turn the intuitive goal of "learning from examples" into a concrete optimization problem. By minimizing the average loss on observed data, we create a proxy for minimizing the true risk on unseen data.
concepts.recap_md: - ERM minimizes the average loss $\mathcal{L}$ over a finite training dataset of size $N$.

slots.motivation: ERM provides a formal mathematical framework to turn the intuitive goal of "learning from examples" into a concrete optimization problem. By minimizing the average loss on observed data, we create a proxy for minimizing the true risk on unseen data.
slots.key_passage: - ERM minimizes the average loss $\mathcal{L}$ over a finite training dataset of size $N$.

concepts.title: Maximum Likelihood Learning
concepts.one_liner: Maximum likelihood learning is an interpretation of ERM that seeks the hypothesis $f$ assigning the highest probability to the observed training data.
concepts.motivation_md: Maximum likelihood learning provides a probabilistic justification for specific loss functions. It allows us to frame learning as finding the model parameters that make the observed data most probable.
concepts.recap_md: - It selects the model $f$ that maximizes the probability of the observed outputs given the inputs.

slots.motivation: Maximum likelihood learning provides a probabilistic justification for specific loss functions. It allows us to frame learning as finding the model parameters that make the observed data most probable.
slots.key_passage: - It selects the model $f$ that maximizes the probability of the observed outputs given the inputs.

concepts.title: Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) Learning
concepts.one_liner: Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) learning infers the most probable hypothesis given the training data by combining a likelihood function with a prior distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: MAP learning allows us to incorporate prior knowledge or beliefs about which hypotheses are more likely before seeing any data, which can help regularize models and prevent overfitting.
concepts.recap_md: - MAP learning maximizes the posterior probability $p(f | \text{data})$.

slots.motivation: MAP learning allows us to incorporate prior knowledge or beliefs about which hypotheses are more likely before seeing any data, which can help regularize models and prevent overfitting.
slots.key_passage: - MAP learning maximizes the posterior probability $p(f | \text{data})$.

concepts.title: Linear Least-Squares Regression
concepts.one_liner: Linear least-squares regression models the relationship between variables using a linear function that minimizes the sum of squared differences between predictions and targets.
concepts.content:
One of the simplest learning problems is known as linear least-squares regression. In this setting, we aim to model the relationship between two variables, $x$ and $y$, with a line. For example, we might train a model on observed examples of {`temperature outside`, `number of people at the beach`} pairs, denoted as $\{x^{(i)},y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. At test time, this model can be applied to predict the $y$ value of a new query $x'$, as shown in (see figure: The goal of learning is to use the training data to predict the $y$ value of the test query. In our example we find that for every 1 degree increase in temperature, we can expect $\sim 10$ more...).

Our hypothesis space is linear functions of the form $\hat{y} = f_{\theta}(x) = \theta_1 x + \theta_0$, parameterized by $\theta_0, \theta_1 \in \mathbb{R}$. Our objective is the $L_2$ loss, where $(\hat{y}^{(i)} - y^{(i)})^2$ should be small for all training examples:

$$\begin{aligned}
    J(\theta) &= \sum_i \mathcal{L}(\hat{y}^{(i)}, y^{(i)})\\
    &\quad \mathcal{L}(\hat{y}, y) = (\hat{y} - y)^2 \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad L_2 \text{ loss}
\end{aligned}$$

The full learning problem is $\theta^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^N (\theta_1 x^{(i)} + \theta_0 - y^{(i)})^2$. This can be rewritten in matrix form as $J(\theta) = (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\theta)^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\theta)$ with:

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X} = 
 \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & x^{(1)}  \\
    1 & x^{(2)} \\
    \vdots & \vdots \\
    1 & x^{(N)}
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
\mathbf{y} = 
 \begin{bmatrix}
    y^{(1)}  \\
    y^{(2)} \\
    \vdots \\
    y^{(N)}
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
\theta = 
 \begin{bmatrix}
    \theta_0 \\
    \theta_1
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}$$

Since $J$ is a quadratic form, we solve for $\theta^*$ by finding where the derivative $\frac{\partial J(\theta)}{\partial \theta} = 2(\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X} \theta - \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y})$ is zero. This yields the closed-form solution:
$$\theta^* = (\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y}.$$

The $\theta^*$ defines the best fitting line to our data (see figure: A best fit line is a visualization of a function $f_{\theta}$, that predicts the $y$-value for each input $x$-value.).

(see figure: Linear regression finds a line that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.)
concepts.motivation_md: Linear least-squares regression provides a simple, interpretable, and mathematically tractable way to predict continuous values. It serves as a foundational model for understanding more complex regression techniques.
concepts.recap_md: - It uses a linear hypothesis space $\hat{y} = \theta_1 x + \theta_0$ and minimizes the $L_2$ (squared) loss.

slots.key_passage: - It uses a linear hypothesis space $\hat{y} = \theta_1 x + \theta_0$ and minimizes the $L_2$ (squared) loss.

    &\quad \mathcal{L}(\hat{y}, y) = (\hat{y} - y)^2 \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad L_2 \text{ loss}
\end{aligned}$$

The full learning problem is $\theta^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \sum_{i=1}^N (\theta_1 x^{(i)} + \theta_0 - y^{(i)})^2$. This can be rewritten in matrix form as $J(\theta) = (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\theta)^\mathsf{T}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\theta)$ with:

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{X} = 
 \begin{bmatrix}
    1 & x^{(1)}  \\
    1 & x^{(2)} \\
    \vdots & \vdots \\
    1 & x^{(N)}
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
\mathbf{y} = 
 \begin{bmatrix}
    y^{(1)}  \\
    y^{(2)} \\
    \vdots \\
    y^{(N)}
\end{bmatrix}
\quad
\theta = 
 \begin{bmatrix}
    \theta_0 \\
    \theta_1
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}$$

Since $J$ is a quadratic form, we solve for $\theta^*$ by finding where the derivative $\frac{\partial J(\theta)}{\partial \theta} = 2(\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X} \theta - \mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y})$ is zero. This yields the closed-form solution:
$$\theta^* = (\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{y}.$$

The $\theta^*$ defines the best fitting line to our data (see figure: A best fit line is a visualization of a function $f_{\theta}$, that predicts the $y$-value for each input $x$-value.).

(see figure: Linear regression finds a line that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.)

concepts.title: Program Induction
concepts.one_liner: Program induction is a broad class of learning algorithms where the hypothesis space consists of computer programs, such as all possible Python programs within a certain length.
concepts.content: Program induction is one of the broadest classes of learning algorithm. In this setting, our hypothesis space may be all Python programs. Unlike linear least-squares, where the learned function is an algebraic expression mapping $x$ to $y$ via two scalar parameters (see figure: Linear regression finds a line that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.), program induction involves searching over the space of all possible Python programs (within some max length) (see figure: Python program induction finds a Python program that predicts the training data's $y$-values from its $x$-values.). This represents a much harder search problem than finding a few scalars.
concepts.motivation_md: Program induction allows for learning extremely complex, algorithmic relationships that cannot be captured by simple mathematical formulas, though it introduces significant search and generalization challenges.
concepts.recap_md: - The hypothesis space consists of programs (e.g., Python code) rather than fixed-form mathematical equations.

concepts.title: One-Hot Code
concepts.one_liner: A one-hot code represents class labels as a $K$-dimensional vector where exactly one element is 1 and the others are 0.
concepts.content:
To represent class labels, a convenient representation is to let $\mathbf{y}$ be a $K$-dimensional vector, for $K$ possible classes, with $y_k = 1$ if $\mathbf{y}$ represents class $k$, and $y_k = 0$ otherwise. This representation is called a one-hot code, since just one element of the vector is on ("hot"). Each class has a unique one-hot code.

An example of one-hot codes for representing $K$=5 different classes:

[FIGURE:b8af1eed48fae94a | A diagram illustrating one-hot encoding for $K$ classes. Three vertical vectors of length 5 are shown, labeled 'class: 1', '2', and 'K'. In the vector for class 1, the first cell is black...]
concepts.motivation_md: One-hot encoding converts categorical labels into a numerical format that can be used in mathematical optimization and loss functions like cross-entropy.
concepts.recap_md: - A label is represented as a vector where the index of the correct class is set to 1 and all other indices are 0.

concepts.title: 0-1 Loss
concepts.one_liner: The 0-1 loss function evaluates to 1 for any misclassification and 0 for a correct prediction.
concepts.motivation_md: The 0-1 loss directly measures the error rate (the number of mistakes), which is often the ultimate metric of interest in classification tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - It assigns a penalty of 1 for any incorrect prediction and 0 for correct ones.

concepts.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
concepts.one_liner: Cross-entropy loss is a continuous and differentiable loss function commonly used for classification tasks.
concepts.motivation_md: Cross-entropy loss provides a smooth, differentiable surface for optimization via gradient descent, unlike the discrete 0-1 loss, while maintaining a clear probabilistic interpretation.
concepts.recap_md: - It measures the difference between the true distribution (one-hot label) and the predicted probability distribution.

concepts.title: Reinforcement Learning
concepts.one_liner: Reinforcement learning involves a learner trying to maximize a reward function that explicitly measures the quality of the learned function's output.
concepts.content: In reinforcement learning, we suppose that we are given a reward function that explicitly measures the quality of the learned function's output. To be precise, a reward function is a mapping from outputs to scores: $r: 	extcal{Y} ightarrow 	extbb{R}$. The learner tries to come up with a function that maximizes rewards. This kind of learning is becoming an important part of computer vision, especially in the context of vision for robots.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a framework for learning when the goal is to maximize a numerical reward signal rather than just matching specific target labels.
concepts.recap_md: - A reward function $r: 	extcal{Y} ightarrow 	extbb{R}$ maps outputs to numerical scores.

concepts.title: Three Key Ingredients of Learning
concepts.one_liner: A learning algorithm consists of three key ingredients: an objective, a hypothesis space, and an optimizer.
concepts.content:
A learning algorithm consists of three key ingredients:

1. Objective: What does it mean for the learner to succeed, or, at least, to perform well?

2. Hypothesis Space: What is the set of possible mappings from inputs to outputs that we will we search over?

3. Optimizer: How, exactly, do we search the hypothesis space for a specific mapping that maximizes the objective?

These three ingredients, when applied to large amounts of data, and run on sufficient hardware (referred to as compute) can do amazing things. Often the data and compute turn out to be more important than the algorithms themselves.

[FIGURE:606f041122e8e0fc | A block diagram representing a machine learning system. 'Data' flows into a central 'Learner' box from the left, and 'Compute' flows in from the bottom. The 'Learner' box contains three components...]
concepts.motivation_md: Breaking down learning into these components allows researchers to systematically design and analyze different machine learning systems.

concepts.title: Objective (Learning Ingredient)
concepts.one_liner: The objective defines what it means for the learner to succeed or perform well.
concepts.content: The objective defines what it means for the learner to succeed, or, at least, to perform well.
concepts.motivation_md: Without a clear objective, there is no way to measure progress or determine which model parameters are better than others.
concepts.recap_md: - It specifies the criteria for successful learning performance.

slots.motivation: Without a clear objective, there is no way to measure progress or determine which model parameters are better than others.

concepts.title: Hypothesis Space
concepts.one_liner: The hypothesis space is the set of all possible mappings from inputs to outputs that a learner considers.
concepts.content: The hypothesis space is the set of possible mappings from inputs to outputs that we will we search over. It can be described by a set $\textcal{F}$ of all the possible functions under consideration by the learner. For example, one hypothesis space might be "all mappings from $\textbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \textbb{R}$" and another could be "all functions $\textbb{R} \times \textbb{R} \rightarrow \textbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ that satisfy the conditions of being a distance metric." Commonly, we will not just specify the hypothesis space, but also how we parameterize the space. For example, we may say that our parameterized hypothesis space is $y = \theta_1 x + \theta_0$, where $\theta_0$ and $\theta_1$ are the parameters. This corresponds to the space of affine functions from $\textbb{R} \rightarrow \textbb{R}$. Different parameterizations of the same space are not equivalent because optimizers and objectives may treat them differently. To fully define a learning algorithm, it is important to specify how the hypothesis space is parameterized.
concepts.motivation_md: It restricts the search for a solution to a manageable set of functions that are appropriate for the problem at hand.
concepts.recap_md: - It represents the set $\textcal{F}$ of all functions the learner can potentially choose.

concepts.title: Optimizer (Learning Ingredient)
concepts.one_liner: The optimizer is the method used to search the hypothesis space for a mapping that maximizes the objective.
concepts.content: The optimizer determines how, exactly, we search the hypothesis space for a specific mapping that maximizes the objective.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides the computational mechanism to actually find the best function within the hypothesis space according to the objective.
concepts.recap_md: - It is the search strategy used to find the optimal mapping.

concepts.title: Learned Function
concepts.one_liner: A learned function is the algorithm produced by a learner that maps inputs to outputs.
concepts.content: A learner outputs an algorithm, $f: \textcal{X} \rightarrow \textcal{Y}$, which maps inputs, $\mathbf{x} \in \textcal{X}$, to outputs, $\mathbf{y} \in \textcal{Y}$. Commonly, $f$ is referred to as the learned function.
concepts.motivation_md: The learned function is the final product of the training process, used to make predictions on new data.
concepts.recap_md: - It is the mapping $f: \textcal{X} \rightarrow \textcal{Y}$ produced by the learning process.

slots.motivation: The learned function is the final product of the training process, used to make predictions on new data.
slots.key_passage: - It is the mapping $f: \textcal{X} \rightarrow \textcal{Y}$ produced by the learning process.

concepts.title: Loss Function
concepts.one_liner: A loss function scores model outputs or compares them to target answers to guide the optimization process.
concepts.content: The objective that the learner optimizes is typically a function that scores model outputs, $\textcal{L}: \textcal{Y} \rightarrow \textbb{R}$, or compares model outputs to target answers, $\textcal{L}: \textcal{Y} \times \textcal{Y} \rightarrow \textbb{R}$. We will interchangeably call this $\textcal{L}$ either the objective function, the loss function, or the loss. A loss almost always refers to an objective we seek to minimize, whereas an objective function can describe objectives we seek to minimize as well as those we seek to maximize.
concepts.motivation_md: It quantifies the error or performance of a model, providing a numerical value that the optimizer can use to improve the function.
concepts.recap_md: - The term "loss" specifically implies an objective that should be minimized.

concepts.title: Overparameterized Models
concepts.one_liner: Overparameterized models use more parameters than the minimum necessary to fit the training data.
concepts.content: Overparameterized models, where you use more parameters than the minimum necessary to fit the data, are especially important in modern computer vision; most neural networks are overparameterized.
concepts.motivation_md: Overparameterization allows models to have the flexibility needed to learn complex patterns in large datasets.
concepts.recap_md: - These models contain more parameters than are strictly required to fit the data.
